name: Joan of Arc
kicker: Peasant girl who led French troops · Later canonized a saint
briefing: At about 17, a peasant girl named Joan of Arc told France’s future king that heavenly visions had sent her to save the country from England. Wearing armor and carrying her own banner, she led French troops to break the Siege of Orléans in 1429, turning the tide of the Hundred Years’ War. Captured a year later, she was convicted of heresy by an English-backed court and burned at the stake in 1431 — but the Catholic Church later declared her innocent and made her a saint.
answerHtml: Joan of Arc (or Saint Joan of Arc, Jeanne d’Arc; prompt on Joan or Jeanne alone)

tossups.p: While imprisoned at Beaurevoir Castle, this woman tried to escape by jumping from a tower some 70 feet high into a dry moat. Earlier, she had told France’s uncrowned heir that heavenly voices, including those of Saints Michael, Catherine, and Margaret, had sent her to save the kingdom.
tossups.r: This peasant girl led French troops to break the Siege of Orléans in 1429. For 10 points, name this teenager who was later burned at the stake and eventually made a saint.

tossups.p: An English-backed court partly convicted this woman of heresy over her choice to wear men’s clothing, since heresy alone required a repeat offense to carry the death penalty. Burgundian forces captured this woman at the Siege of Compiègne [“kom-pyen”] in 1430 and later sold her to the English.
tossups.r: This commander had escorted Charles VII to Reims for his coronation the year before. For 10 points, name this French peasant who was burned at the stake in 1431.

tossups.p: Years after her death, a woman named Claude des Armoises pretended to be this person, claiming she had secretly survived. A later church trial, held about 25 years after her death, declared this person innocent and a martyr.
tossups.r: This commander broke the English siege of Orléans in 1429. For 10 points, name this French peasant girl, eventually canonized a saint by the Catholic Church.

tossups.p: This commander reportedly pushed French captains to make greater use of artillery and cannons during sieges. Said to have experienced visions of Saints Michael, Catherine, and Margaret, this teenager left her village of Domrémy [“doh-ray-MEE”] to find France’s uncrowned heir.
tossups.r: This leader helped crown Charles VII at Reims. For 10 points, name this peasant girl who led French troops during the Hundred Years’ War.

tossups.p: This woman’s connection to Saint Michael is one reason he is considered a patron saint of France. Historians still study the unusually detailed trial transcripts kept from this woman’s 1431 trial, among the best-documented records to survive from the Middle Ages.
tossups.r: This commander was burned at the stake after being convicted of heresy. For 10 points, name this teenage French peasant who broke the Siege of Orléans.

tossups.p: Rather than fighting hand-to-hand, this commander mostly rode into battle wearing armor and carrying her own banner to inspire French troops. Burgundian forces captured this commander at Compiègne and sold her to the English, who put her on trial at Rouen [“roo-AHN”].
tossups.r: This peasant girl helped crown Charles VII at Reims in 1429. For 10 points, name this French teenager burned at the stake for heresy in 1431.

tossups.p: This teenager first approached Charles VII while he was still only France’s uncrowned “Dauphin,” convincing him that heavenly visions had sent her to save the kingdom. This commander then led troops that broke the long English siege of Orléans in 1429.
tossups.r: This peasant was burned at the stake two years later. For 10 points, name this French commander from the Hundred Years’ War, later made a Catholic saint.

tossups.p: This woman tried to escape captivity at Beaurevoir Castle by leaping from a high tower into a dry moat below. A posthumous trial about 25 years after her death declared this woman innocent of all charges and a martyr.

tossups.p: This teenager encouraged French commanders to rely more on artillery, including in the fighting that finally broke the English siege of Orléans. A few years after her death, a woman named Claude des Armoises falsely claimed to be this person.

trap.title: The heroine, not the war
trap.body: Joan of Arc is one of the most famous figures in the Hundred Years’ War, but she is a different answer from the war itself, from the king she helped crown (Charles VII), and from the siege she’s most famous for breaking (the Siege of Orléans). Real answer lines for Joan of Arc reject the war’s name, and the reverse is true too.
trap.fix: If the question asks to “name this war” or spans more than a century, say the war. If it asks for the peasant girl, soldier, or saint who heard visions and led troops, say Joan of Arc. “Just Joan” or “Jeanne” alone only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Joan of Arc (or Saint Joan of Arc, Jeanne d’Arc; prompt on Joan or Jeanne alone)
